query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Heat treatment that induces a gradient nanocrystalline subsurface in the FeNiCrCoCu coating will promote the development of a continuous, dense oxide (glaze) layer during high-temperature sliding, thereby improving wear resistance and accommodating plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating with a relatively homogeneous, coarse or moderately refined microstructure and non-uniform in situ oxide formation.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition high-temperature annealing treatment (e.g., a hold at an intermediate temperature below the melting point but high enough to drive partial recrystallization) to induce a depth-dependent refinement, forming a top nanocrystalline (NC) tribo-layer transitioning to an ultra-fine grained (UFG) region beneath.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (typically in the 600–800 °C regime) in ambient (or controlled oxidizing) atmosphere where tribo-oxidation can occur.
generation.structural_mediator: A gradient nanostructured (NC-to-UFG) subsurface that facilitates gradual stress relaxation and simultaneously promotes a continuous, dense oxide glaze layer.
generation.mechanism: The refined NC layer at the immediate surface enhances hardness and elevates the H/E and H3/E2 ratios, while the gradual grain size increase underneath minimizes sharp strain demarcations during sliding. In parallel, the enhanced grain boundary density accelerates tribo-oxidation kinetics to form a stable glaze layer that prevents direct adhesive contact. Together, these factors reduce abrasive damage and delamination under high-temperature wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the annealed coating should exhibit a markedly lower wear rate (by at least an order of magnitude similar to trends seen in nanohierarchical architectures) and reduced groove formation with fewer wear debris under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: The unannealed FeNiCrCoCu coating exhibiting less gradient structural evolution and a sporadic, discontinuous oxide layer.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in high-temperature regimes (≥600 °C) where oxidation kinetics are favorable, but may not be effective at significantly lower temperatures where oxide formation is minimal.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature and time parameters for optimal gradient formation in FeNiCrCoCu are uncertain, and the balance between softening and oxide layer stability must be tuned.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical substrates: one set receives the controlled post-deposition annealing to develop a gradient nanostructure and the other remains as-deposited. Subject both to identical high-temperature (600–800 °C) sliding wear tests in the same oxidizing environment.
measurements: Wear rate (mm3/Nm) via profilometry
Coefficient of friction (COF)
Cross-sectional microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to verify gradient structure and glaze layer continuity
Nanoindentation to measure local H and E values
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and improved stress accommodation (as indicated by more uniform H/E profiles and thicker, continuous glaze layers) compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-temperature corrosion is chemical deterioration of a material (typically a metal) as a result of heating. This non-galvanic form of corrosion can occur when a metal is subjected to a hot atmosphere containing oxygen, sulfur ("sulfidation"), or other compounds capable of oxidizing (or assisting the oxidation of) the material concerned. For example, materials used in aerospace, power generation, and even in car engines must resist sustained periods at high temperature, during which they may be exposed to an atmosphere containing the potentially highly-corrosive products of combustion. Some products of high-temperature corrosion can potentially be turned to the advantage of the engineer. The formation of oxides on stainless steels, for example, can provide a protective layer preventing further atmospheric attack, allowing for a material to be used for sustained periods at both room and high temperatures in hostile conditions. Such high-temperature corrosion products, in the form of compacted oxide layer glazes, prevent or reduce wear during high-temperature sliding contact of metallic (or metallic and ceramic) surfaces. paper_did: Prepared a single‐phase, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy via arc melting, homogenization, rolling, and recrystallization; the samples were polished to remove any pre‐existing deformation layers.

Conducted dry, reciprocating sliding wear tests using sapphire spheres under mild loading (2 N, 0.5 mm/s, 12 mm stroke) across a range of cycle numbers (from 0.5 up to 1000 cycles) at room temperature.
Utilized cross‐sectional techniques (SEM, FIB, TEM, TKD, CS-EBSD, EDS) to characterize the evolution of subsurface microstructure during sliding.
paper_reported: A surprisingly thick subsurface deformation layer (8–14 µm) forms even after a single stroke, comprised of a fine nanocrystalline top layer and an underlying banded region.
Twin formation and localized dislocation rearrangement play a decisive role in the development and thickness of the deformation layer, with twin fragmentation contributing to nanocrystallization.
Friction coefficient behavior evolves in three regimes, with initial adhesive wear, material transfer (including oxide-rich layers) and changes in wear mechanisms being reported.
paper_proposed: The study suggests that a deeper understanding of these tribologically induced microstructural changes in CoCrFeMnNi can inspire the design of new high-entropy alloys with tailored compositions and surface structures optimized for tribological applications.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Pre-sliding annealing to increase nanotwin density in the FeNiCrCoCu coating improves wear resistance and moderates subsurface deformation by promoting homogeneous plasticity at high temperature.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A thin, as-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate with a conventional, rapidly quenched microstructure (baseline: relatively coarse grain structure with low pre-existing twin density).
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a controlled post-deposition, high-temperature (e.g., ~800°C for 1 hour) annealing treatment in an inert atmosphere designed to promote the formation of nanotwins and refine the near-surface grain structure prior to sliding.
hypotheses.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime (e.g., operating temperatures of 400–600°C) under tribological loads similar to those in the baseline test.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: An increased density of coherent twin boundaries and a refined, nanocrystalline surface layer that develop during the anneal.
hypotheses.mechanism: The pre-induced twin boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion and effectively distribute shear stresses during sliding, thereby reducing localized deformation and delaying the onset of wear-associated phenomena such as adhesive material transfer and abrupt microstructural fragmentation. This leads to a more uniform deformation layer even in high temperature conditions where thermal activation might otherwise promote severe wear.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the annealed coating is predicted to exhibit a lower wear rate and less severe localized subsurface deformation (for instance, a reduction in wear volume by an estimated 20–40% and a more homogeneous deformation profile), observable in post-test cross-sectional microscopy.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-sprayed and rapidly quenched FeNiCrCoCu coating without any post-deposition annealing.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism should hold in the high-temperature regime (above ~400°C) where thermally activated twin-related processes and homogeneous plasticity can be exploited; it may not apply at ambient temperature or in regimes where oxidation dominates entirely.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvement in wear resistance is expected, the precise magnitude of improvement and the sensitivity to annealing parameters (temperature/time) are uncertain.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Inducing controlled Cu-rich nanoprecipitate formation by modifying the post-deposition cooling rate in the FeNiCrCoCu coating will improve wear resistance by hindering localized deformation under high-temperature sliding.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A thin FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating produced by rapid cooling (as-sprayed), resulting in a metastable, single-phase solid solution with minimal phase segregation.
hypotheses.intervention: Replace the rapid quench with a slower furnace-cooling post-deposition treatment to allow controlled phase separation and the precipitation of nanoscale Cu-rich particles uniformly distributed in the matrix.
hypotheses.conditions: High-temperature operating regime during sliding (e.g., 400–600°C) where moderate diffusion permits precipitate stability without coarsening.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The formation of finely dispersed Cu-rich nanoprecipitates that act to pin dislocation motion and obstruct the development of highly localized shear bands.
hypotheses.mechanism: The nanometer-scale Cu-rich precipitates impede dislocation glide and delay the formation of localized deformation zones. This precipitation strengthening leads to a more even distribution of plastic strain during high-temperature sliding, reducing wear and microstructural degradation relative to a homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The slower-cooled coating is expected to display a reduction in wear rate (e.g., a 10–30% decrease in wear volume) and exhibit a less pronounced localized deformation layer upon post-test microstructural evaluation compared to the rapidly quenched baseline.
hypotheses.baseline: The conventional as-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating cooled rapidly to retain a single-phase, homogeneous microstructure.
hypotheses.boundary: The benefits of precipitate formation are predicted to manifest under high-temperature sliding conditions where diffusion is sufficient to form and stabilize nanoprecipitates; at lower temperatures, the imbalance in phase kinetics might render the intervention ineffective.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The kinetics of Cu-rich precipitate formation and its quantitative impact on wear resistance are somewhat uncertain, and the optimum cooling rate must be empirically determined.

hypotheses.material_initial_state: A thin, smooth, as-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate with a uniform surface finish (baseline condition).
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a laser surface texturing process to create a regular array of micro-dimples (e.g., tens of micrometers in diameter and depth) on the top surface of the coating prior to high-temperature sliding tests.
hypotheses.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., operating temperatures above 400°C) where oxidation is thermally activated and where contact stresses produce both adhesive and abrasive wear mechanisms.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Periodic micro-dimples that alter the effective contact area by locally reducing contact pressure, and that serve as reservoirs for lubricious oxides and debris which form under high-temperature conditions.
hypotheses.mechanism: The micro-dimples reduce peak local stresses and promote a more distributed stress field during sliding, while simultaneously trapping oxide debris that can act as a lubricious layer. This leads to reduced adhesive wear and limits the severity of localized deformation (such as concentrated twin fragmentation or shear banding) in the subsurface region.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to the smooth baseline coating, the laser-textured coating should exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and a reduced wear rate (potentially a reduction of ~15–30% in wear volume). Microstructural analysis is expected to reveal a more uniform subsurface deformation layer with reduced evidence of localized deformation damage.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating with a flat, untextured surface.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism should be effective in regimes where high temperature fosters oxide formation; however, if the operating temperature is too low to create a stable oxide or too high causing rapid oxide spallation, the benefits may diminish.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact influence of micro-dimple geometry (size, depth, density) on the wear and deformation mechanisms is uncertain and requires optimization.

paper_did: Synthesized two complex concentrated alloys (CCAs): Ni3X (Ni75(AlNbTiV)25) and NiX (Ni50(AlNbTiV)50) via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering.

Characterized the microstructures using BF‐TEM, SAED, HAADF-STEM, and EDS mapping to reveal a nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation, including nano‐coupled grains and nanoprecipitates.
Conducted systematic wear tests from room temperature to 800 °C, measuring wear rates, coefficients of friction, hardness, and nanoindentation parameters (H/E and H3/E2) on worn surfaces.

Identified that the superior wear resistance in NiX is due to adaptive friction interface protection via the formation of a gradient recrystallized tribo-layer at room temperature and a continuous nanocrystalline glaze layer at high temperatures.
paper_reported: NiX achieved ultralow wear rates (on the order of 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁶ mm³/Nm) across the temperature range, outperforming conventional alloys, wear‐resistant steels, and other high‐performance systems.

The paper demonstrated that a nanohierarchical architecture with compositional undulation enables progressive stress relaxation by forming a two‐layer (nanocrystalline and ultra‐fine grained) tribo-layer, which helps in accommodating elastic–plastic deformation during sliding.
It reported that at elevated temperatures (600–800 °C), a dense and stable glaze layer forms on NiX, significantly reducing adhesive and oxidative wear compared to Ni3X.
It provided mechanistic insights into how grain refinement, gradient structural transition, and controlled tribo-oxidation collectively enhance wear resistance.
paper_proposed: The paper proposes that tailoring wear properties through the engineering of multicomponent heterostructures—specifically by designing adaptive friction interfaces with gradient nanostructured layers and continuous glaze layers—offers a practical route to ultrawear‐resistant alloys.

It suggests that further detailed simulations and experiments are needed to confirm the mechanisms driving the formation of the nanohierarchical architecture (e.g., the multicomponent solutal response during processing).

paper_did: Fabricated a high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating on SS-304 steel using a microwave hybrid heating process with a ball‐milled powder blend of five elemental powders (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, and Cu) in equal 20 wt.% proportions.
Preheated the ball‐milled powders and deposited them on the substrate using a 900 W, 2.45 GHz microwave system with charcoal employed as a susceptor to assist energy absorption.

Exposed the microwave‐cladded samples to thermal treatment in air at 800 °C for up to ten weeks and performed subsequent microstructural (SEM, optical microscopy, XRD), hardness (Vickers), corrosion (3.5 wt% NaCl immersion), and wear (pin‐on‐disc under ASTM G99 conditions) evaluations.
paper_reported: The formation of a uniformly distributed cladding layer that, upon prolonged thermal exposure, developed a protective Cr2O3 layer along with a high-entropy spinel oxide ((Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4) which contributed to enhanced wear and corrosion resistance.
An increase in surface hardness was reported, attributed to the formation of harder phases during microwave cladding, with improved thermostability being noted under high-temperature conditions.
Microstructural analysis revealed overall coating homogeneity although some micro-cracks appeared at the coating–substrate interface – likely due to differential cooling and residual stress effects.
paper_proposed: The study suggests that HEA coatings produced via microwave cladding have potential for SOFC interconnect applications, implying that further optimization of cladding parameters (such as preheating, irradiation time, and powder composition uniformity) could further enhance properties.
There is an implicit proposal to delve deeper into the mechanisms behind protective oxide formation and the mitigation of microstructural defects to improve long-term thermal and wear performance.

paper_did: Microwave cladding was used to deposit a high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating made from equal‐wt% Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, and Cu powders onto an SS‑304 steel substrate using microwave hybrid heating (900 W at 2.45 GHz) with charcoal as a susceptor.
Prior to cladding, the elemental powders were ball-milled (with a fixed speed of 200 rpm and a ball-to-powder ratio of 5:1) and preheated to remove moisture, then uniformly spread on the substrate.
The cladded samples underwent thermal exposure in air for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C to promote phase evolution.

A variety of characterizations were performed including SEM imaging for microstructural analysis, XRD phase analysis, Vickers hardness measurements, wear testing using a pin‐on‐disc setup (with specified sliding speed, distance, and load), and corrosion testing via immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
paper_reported: The formation of a uniform cladding layer on SS‑304 was confirmed, with the microstructure showing a homogeneous dispersion of the HEA particles and evidence of metallurgical bonding despite some micro‐cracks at the interface.

Upon thermal exposure at 800 °C, protective oxide layers were formed – notably a Cr2O3 layer and a high-entropy spinel coating ((Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4) – which contributed to enhanced hardness, improved wear resistance, and corrosion protection for potential SOFC interconnect applications.
The study highlighted that microwave cladding leads to the development of harder phases and favorable microstructural features that can improve the mechanical and chemical stability of the substrate.
paper_proposed: Future work is suggested to optimize the microwave cladding process parameters (such as irradiation duration, preheating time, and powder loading) to further control the microstructural homogeneity and adhesion quality of the coating.

Investigations into the development of improved barrier layers (for example, by fine-tuning the protective oxide or spinel phase formation) to better resist wear and corrosion under harsh, high-temperature environments were also indicated.
There is an implicit proposal to explore further modifications of the HEA composition and processing conditions to tailor the coatings for enhanced performance in SOFC interconnect applications.

paper_did: Used machine learning (MLR, BPNN, RF) to correlate principal element content with tensile strength and predict an optimal Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 composition.
Validated the ML prediction with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of tension and compression tests at various temperatures (77 K, 300 K, 600 K, 900 K) and different composition ratios.
Analyzed microstructural evolution during deformation including dislocation nail formation, twinning, and slip behavior in both single crystal and polycrystalline HEAs.
Investigated the effect of applying an HEA coating on a Ni matrix to modify the tensile and compressive responses and reduce tension–compression asymmetry.
paper_reported: The optimal composition Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 HEA achieves a tensile strength of ~28.25 GPa, with MD simulation verifying the ML prediction within 0.5% error.

Tensile strength in FeNiCrCoCu HEAs increases with higher Fe and Ni content, while variations in Co and Cu affect the strength non‐linearly, and the temperature has a strong detrimental effect on tensile strength.
Distinct tension–compression asymmetry arises from mechanisms such as dislocation pinning, twin formation, and slip surface evolution; compressive strength is generally higher than tensile strength.

paper_did: Fabricated copper surface metal matrix composites by friction stir processing (FSP) on copper plates with machined grooves filled with AlCoCrCuFe high-entropy alloy (HEA) particles at different volume fractions (5%, 10%, and 15%).
Performed microstructural characterization (optical microscopy and SEM), hardness measurements, and tensile tests on the FSPed composites.

Conducted systematic pin‐on‐disc wear tests (following ASTM G99) under various sliding conditions (varying applied load, sliding speed, and sliding distance) and determined both the wear rate and the coefficient of friction (CoF).
Analyzed worn surfaces via SEM to correlate the improved wear resistance of HEA‐reinforced composites with enhanced hardness, load‐carrying capability, and a refined grain structure.
paper_reported: The addition of HEA reinforcement to copper significantly reduces the wear rate compared to pure copper, although it increases the coefficient of friction.
Improved wear resistance is mainly attributed to an increase in hardness and a fine, refined microstructure resulting from the FSP process.
Wear rate correlates positively with load, sliding speed, and sliding distance, whereas the CoF generally increases with higher HEA content and under more severe sliding conditions.
SEM analysis of the worn surfaces confirms that higher HEA percentages produce less severe surface damage, substantiating the load‐carrying and microstructural benefits of HEA addition.
paper_proposed: By incorporating HEA reinforcement through FSP, the work suggests a viable route to enhance copper’s surface wear resistance, implying future studies could optimize reinforcement levels and processing parameters.
The study hints at further exploration into tailoring the microstructure and interfacial properties to better balance wear resistance with other mechanical properties.

paper_reported: Incorporation of 32% WC into the HEA improved hardness (from about 470 HV to approximately 562 HV) but led to an inhomogeneous distribution of hard phases and microstructural defects such as porosity and occasional cracks.

paper_did: Fabricated Al1.8CrCuFeNi2 high‐entropy alloy coatings with varying TiC contents (10, 20, and 30 wt.%) by laser cladding on 65 Mn high‐carbon spring steel.

Characterized the coatings’ phase structure using XRD and microstructure using SEM/EDS, documenting the transition from a single BCC phase (at 10 wt.% TiC) to the appearance of TiC agglomerated particles (at 20 and 30 wt.% TiC) along with grain refinement.

Measured microhardness and conducted dry sliding wear tests (under a 100 N load at room temperature for 30 and 120 minutes) to show that increasing TiC content leads to enhanced hardness and significantly reduced wear loss through dispersion strengthening and grain refinement.
paper_reported: The 10 wt.% TiC coating maintained a single BCC phase with high crystallinity and uniform element distribution, whereas higher TiC contents led to the formation of TiC-agglomerated particles and more refined, even if slightly coarser, grain structures.

The improved hardness and wear resistance were attributed to two mechanisms: dispersion strengthening (from the hard TiC phases acting as load-bearing particles) and fine-grain strengthening (grain refinement leading to higher dislocation barriers).
Among the coatings studied, the 30 wt.% TiC composite coating exhibited the best overall performance in terms of hardness and wear resistance.
paper_proposed: While the paper did not explicitly outline future work, it implies that further optimization in reinforcing strategies (by adjusting ceramic particle content) could be beneficial, paving the way for exploring alternative dispersion methods to boost wear resistance.

paper_did: Fabricated Al1.8CrCuFeNi2 high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coatings with varying contents of TiC (10, 20, and 30 wt.%) using laser cladding onto a 65 Mn high‐carbon spring steel substrate.
Employed a powder feeding system under argon protection with controlled laser parameters, followed by systematic drying and delivery of pre‐prepared HEA powders and TiC additions.

Characterized the coatings extensively via X‐ray diffraction (XRD), energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS), metallographic optical microscopy, microhardness testing, and dry friction wear experiments under specified loads and durations.
paper_reported: At 10 wt.% TiC the coating retained a single BCC solid solution phase, while at 20 wt.% and 30 wt.% TiC, TiC compounds (agglomerated particles) began to form, indicating partial saturation and in situ precipitation.

An increase in TiC content resulted in pronounced grain refinement and a significant increase in microhardness; the 30 wt.% TiC coating exhibited the highest hardness and the lowest measured wear loss.
The improvements in wear resistance were attributed primarily to two mechanisms: grain refinement (fine‐grain strengthening) and dispersion strengthening (load‐bearing by the hard TiC particles).
paper_proposed: While the paper did not explicitly list future work experiments, its discussion implies that further optimization of TiC content and understanding of the interplay between phase formation and wear resistance could be valuable.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of both tungsten and carbon to the FeNiCrCoCu HEA powder to promote the in situ formation of nano-scale tungsten carbide particles during a mild post-cladding heat treatment will improve high-temperature wear resistance by pinning dislocations and impeding micro-crack propagation during sliding.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu HEA thin coating produced via standard laser cladding with a homogeneous single-phase solid solution and no significant carbide dispersions.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the initial powder blend by adding 2–3 wt.% tungsten and 1–2 wt.% carbon. After laser cladding, apply a mild heat treatment that is high enough to drive limited carbide formation without causing undesirable coarsening or dissolution.
hypotheses.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime typically in the 500–700 °C range, where carbide dispersions are thermally stable and effective at impeding deformation.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Evenly distributed nano-scale tungsten carbide (WC or WC-like) precipitates within the HEA matrix, particularly at grain boundaries and within grains.
hypotheses.mechanism: The nano-scale WC precipitates act as strong obstacles to dislocation movement and micro-crack propagation by pinning grain boundaries and blocking slip. Their high hardness and thermal stability help maintain an effective load-bearing network during high-temperature sliding, reducing plastic deformation and wear.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The tungsten and carbon doped, heat-treated coating should show an increase in overall hardness and a measurable decrease in wear loss and microscopic deformation (e.g., shallower wear grooves, fewer micro-cracks) compared to the undoped baseline.
hypotheses.baseline: Standard FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating without tungsten or carbon additions and without subsequent heat treatment to induce carbide formation.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative under high-temperature sliding (500–700 °C) where the in situ formed carbides remain stable; if the temperature exceeds the stability range, carbide dissolution could occur.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise tungsten-to-carbon ratio required for optimal WC formation and the kinetics of carbide precipitation in the HEA matrix remain to be fully determined.

Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests (500–700 °C) and compare the microstructures using TEM/XRD for carbide formation, measure hardness, and quantify wear loss.
measurements: Nano-scale phase analysis (TEM/XRD) to detect WC precipitates
Microhardness measurements at room and high temperature
Wear loss quantification and friction coefficient during sliding
Microscopic examination (SEM) of the wear tracks for crack density and groove depth
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped and heat-treated coatings do not form a significant amount of nano-scale tungsten carbide precipitates or do not exhibit statistically lower wear loss and reduced microscopic deformation compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Employing a two-step laser cladding process to build a graded microstructure—with a nanocrystalline top layer and a comparatively coarser-grained interior—will enhance high-temperature wear resistance and reduce microscopic deformation during sliding by stabilizing a hard, wear-resistant surface.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Conventional FeNiCrCoCu HEA thin coating produced by a single-pass, standard laser cladding process, yielding a relatively uniform microstructure.
hypotheses.intervention: First, deposit a standard laser-clad FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating. hypotheses.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (500–700 °C) where the top surface properties dominate wear behavior and the graded structure can resist deformation and delay crack initiation.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A graded microstructure featuring a top nanocrystalline layer—with a high density of grain boundaries that act as barriers to dislocation movement—and an underlying coarser-grained layer acting as a compliant substrate.
hypotheses.mechanism: The nanocrystalline surface layer enhances hardness and provides a high density of grain boundary barriers that limit dislocation motion and suppress localized plastic deformation, while the underlying coarser structure accommodates strain. hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The graded coating should exhibit significantly lower wear loss, a higher effective hardness at the sliding interface, and less severe microscopic deformation features (e.g., shallower grooves and reduced crack propagation) compared to the conventional single-pass coating.
hypotheses.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings fabricated via a conventional single-pass laser cladding process.

paper_did: Calculated phase diagrams using the CALPHAD approach for over 130,000 candidate equimolar multi‐principal element alloys and applied a stringent credibility filter (fAB = 1) to narrow the data to 4,983 unique systems.
Analyzed the phase stability by classifying alloys into solid solution (SS), intermetallic (IM), or mixed (SS+IM) categories at both the solidus temperature (Tm) and at 600 °C.

Evaluated key properties such as melting temperature (Tm), estimated maximum use temperature (Tuse), density, Young’s modulus, and cost through cumulative distributions, and identified trends with increasing number of alloying elements.
Demonstrated the identification of 51 candidate equimolar alloy systems for high‐temperature structural applications using simple design rules based on the computed phase diagrams.
paper_reported: The surprising result that the fraction of disordered solid solution (SS) alloys decreases with increasing number of alloying elements, contradicting the traditional HEA premise based solely on increased configurational entropy.

A detailed trend showing that single-phase SS alloys are common in lower-component systems (e.g., 3-component alloys) but become rare in higher-component systems, while multi–phase (SS+IM) alloys increase with N.
That extreme property ranges (e.g., for Tm, Tuse, density, and Young’s modulus) narrow as the number of elements increases, with equimolar ternary alloys offering the widest spreads.

A set of design criteria and examples (e.g., alloys with no IM phases at Tm, Tuse ≥ 1000 °C, density ≤ 10 g cm⁻³, Young’s modulus ≥ 100 GPa, and cost ≤ $200 per kg) used to pinpoint promising alloy systems for further study.
paper_proposed: Extending the screening methodology to non‐equimolar compositions in order to capture local compositions with potentially more extreme or tailored properties.
Relaxing the strict fAB = 1 credibility filter in future studies after further experimental validation to include a broader range of candidate alloy systems.

Developing high–throughput experimental techniques that can accommodate the intrinsic microstructural length scales in structural metal alloys to validate and further refine the computational predictions.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A controlled aging heat treatment that induces a fine, nanometer‐scale intermetallic precipitate dispersion within the FeNiCrCoCu solid solution can enhance wear resistance and limit microscopic plastic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-deposited, equimolar FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with a largely homogeneous solid solution microstructure.
hypotheses.intervention: Perform a solution treatment followed by an aging heat treatment (at a temperature below the coating’s solidus but high enough to promote nucleation of intermetallic phases) to precipitate nanoscale intermetallic particles within the solid solution matrix.
hypotheses.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime where the coating is exposed to temperatures approaching its maximum use temperature (e.g., 600–800 °C) under tribological load.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A refined dispersion of nano precipitates within the primary matrix, leading to a dual-phase microstructure with coherent or semi-coherent intermetallic particles.
hypotheses.mechanism: The nanoscale intermetallic precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion and inhibit local plastic flow during sliding. This precipitate hardening mechanism increases local yield strength and suppresses microscopic deformation, thereby reducing wear rate. The presence of these precipitates also refines the grain structure, which is known to contribute to improved mechanical properties. This builds on the paper’s discussion regarding phase stability in multi-component alloys and the competition between disordered solid solution and ordered intermetallic phases (PMC4366518::web::016, PMC4366518::web::020).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A measurable decrease in wear depth and microscopic deformation, with improved hardness and reduced plastic flow in the aged coating compared to the as-deposited baseline. Expected directional improvements are enhanced wear resistance and possibly ~20-30% reduction in wear rate, though the quantitative magnitude is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated, as-deposited equimolar FeNiCrCoCu coating.
hypotheses.boundary: The beneficial effect should be observed in high-temperature sliding tests (600–800 °C) where the precipitates remain stable; excessive aging that leads to coarse intermetallics or embrittlement would negate the improvement.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimal aging temperature and time window to produce the desired nanoscale precipitate distribution are subject to experimental optimization and may vary with slight changes in composition.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Introducing an ultra-thin, reactive interlayer (e.g., titanium) between the FeNiCrCoCu coating and the conventional metal substrate can enhance load transfer and reduce interfacial stresses during high-temperature sliding, thereby improving overall wear resistance and mitigating local deformation.

hypotheses.intervention: Deposit a nanometer-thick titanium (Ti) interlayer on the substrate prior to the deposition of the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
hypotheses.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., 600–800 °C) where differential thermal expansion between the coating and substrate could induce high interfacial stresses.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: An optimized interfacial transition layer with graded composition that promotes chemical bonding and mechanical cohesiveness between the coating and substrate.
hypotheses.mechanism: The Ti interlayer improves adhesion and better accommodates differences in thermal expansion, thereby reducing delamination, crack initiation, and localized plastic deformation at or near the coating–substrate interface. Improved load transfer minimizes interfacial strain concentrations during sliding, which is critical under high-temperature conditions. Elevated temperature studies of coating mechanics have emphasized the importance of interfacial stress distributions (TXT::doitpoms::coating_mechanics/intro::000).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Enhanced wear resistance characterized by reduced delamination and lower interface-related wear, as well as decreased microscopic deformation near the interface compared to the baseline coating. The friction coefficient during sliding is also expected to decrease modestly.
hypotheses.baseline: Directly deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without an interfacial modification.
hypotheses.boundary: This improvement is expected under conditions where the Ti layer remains stable and does not oxidize excessively. Extreme temperatures that degrade the Ti interlayer could invalidate the outcome.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimum thickness and deposition conditions for the Ti interlayer require experimental tuning, and the exact quantitative improvement in wear resistance is uncertain.

hypotheses.mechanism: The pre-formed Cr2O3 tribolayer acts as a solid lubricant, thereby reducing direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding, lowering friction and suppressing severe plastic deformation. This oxide barrier also protects the underlying high-entropy alloy from oxidative degradation during high-temperature service. The concept builds upon the known effectiveness of protective oxide layers in coating systems (see TXT::wikipedia::Thermal_barrier_coating::001 and TXT::wikipedia::Hydrogen_embrittlement::014).

hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise processing parameters (time, temperature) to form the optimal oxide layer without degrading the substrate are yet to be fully defined and could affect quantitative outcomes.

paper_did: Developed a high‐throughput combinatorial approach using CALPHAD to calculate phase diagrams for over 130,000 equimolar multi‐principal element alloy systems (filtered to 5,540 credible cases).

Identified and categorized alloy systems into single-phase solid solutions (SS), intermetallics (IM) and mixed (SS+IM) at both the solidus (Tm) and a lower temperature (600°C), and analyzed how these change with increasing number of components.

Calculated cumulative distributions of key properties (solidus temperature, estimated maximum use temperature Tuse, density, Young’s modulus, and cost) and proposed candidate alloy systems for high‐temperature structural applications.
paper_reported: Found that as the number of alloying elements increases, the probability of obtaining only disordered SS phases decreases (i.e. intermetallic formation becomes more likely), contradicting the classic HEA premise regarding configurational entropy.
Reported that extreme values for properties (melting temperature, Tuse, density, modulus, cost) are generally more accessible in lower‐component (ternary) alloys than in higher‐component systems.
Identified 51 new equimolar alloy systems (with 3–6 base elements) that meet a set of rigorous design criteria for potential high‐temperature structural applications.
paper_proposed: Extending the screening to non‐equimolar alloy compositions to capture local compositions with more extreme property combinations.
Performing further experimental validations—including high‐throughput experimental techniques—to verify the CALPHAD predictions and to handle microstructural length‐scale issues in structural alloys.
Exploring multi‐phase microstructures (rather than striving only for single‐phase alloys) as viable candidates for balancing the competing property requirements of structural metals.

paper_did: Synthesized CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) ingots by arc‐melting, forging, and annealing followed by cold rolling to obtain two distinct microstructures: fine grain (FG, ~2.9 μm) and coarse grain (CG, ~63.4 μm).

Prepared sliding wear test specimens from the processed HEAs and conducted dry sliding friction tests using a hardened Si3N4 ball under varying normal loads (5 N and 30 N) and sliding speeds (1, 5, and 10 mm/s).

Characterized the microstructure using EBSD, measured hardness via nanoindentation, and analyzed worn surfaces with SEM, EDS, and 3D white light interferometry to determine friction coefficients and specific wear rates.
paper_reported: FG samples exhibited higher hardness (~4.9 GPa) and superior wear resistance with lower friction coefficients and reduced specific wear rates compared to CG samples owing to their enhanced surface strength and stable oxide layers.

Under low normal load and sliding speed, adhesive wear dominated, whereas at higher speeds and loads oxidation wear and plastic deformation became prominent, especially in CG samples where the oxide layer was prone to cracking.
The formation of a continuous oxide layer under high load served as a lubricating film to lower friction, although its fracture in CG samples led to increased wear.
paper_proposed: Further exploration of microstructural modifications—such as grain refinement through controlled heat treatments—to enhance wear performance.
Investigations into alternative processing routes and potential compositional modifications (e.g., to stabilize oxidation behavior) to optimize the tribological performance of HEAs.

hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in wear rate is uncertain; the magnitude is expected to be moderate but will depend on the annealing parameters and resultant grain size distribution.

pool.builds_on: This hypothesis builds on the paper’s observations that surface oxidation and subsurface microstructural evolution (such as oxide mixing with nanocrystalline layers) crucially affect friction and wear, and integrates tribological principles of stress modulation through surface texturing.
pool.what_is_new: It proposes a novel surface engineering approach—laser-induced micro-dimpling—to actively control both the local stress state and subsequent oxide formation in a FeNiCrCoCu coating, thereby offering an alternative route to enhancing wear resistance and moderating subsurface deformation in high-temperature applications.

fields.hypothesis: Engineered surface texturing via laser-induced micro-dimples on the FeNiCrCoCu coating will modulate local stress concentrations and promote beneficial oxide film formation, thereby enhancing wear resistance and stabilizing microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
fields.material_initial_state: A thin, smooth, as-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate with a uniform surface finish (baseline condition).
fields.intervention: Apply a laser surface texturing process to create a regular array of micro-dimples (e.g., tens of micrometers in diameter and depth) on the top surface of the coating prior to high-temperature sliding tests.
fields.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., operating temperatures above 400°C) where oxidation is thermally activated and where contact stresses produce both adhesive and abrasive wear mechanisms.
fields.structural_mediator: Periodic micro-dimples that alter the effective contact area by locally reducing contact pressure, and that serve as reservoirs for lubricious oxides and debris which form under high-temperature conditions.
fields.mechanism: The micro-dimples reduce peak local stresses and promote a more distributed stress field during sliding, while simultaneously trapping oxide debris that can act as a lubricious layer. This leads to reduced adhesive wear and limits the severity of localized deformation (such as concentrated twin fragmentation or shear banding) in the subsurface region.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the smooth baseline coating, the laser-textured coating should exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and a reduced wear rate (potentially a reduction of ~15–30% in wear volume). Microstructural analysis is expected to reveal a more uniform subsurface deformation layer with reduced evidence of localized deformation damage.
fields.baseline: The as-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating with a flat, untextured surface.
fields.boundary: This mechanism should be effective in regimes where high temperature fosters oxide formation; however, if the operating temperature is too low to create a stable oxide or too high causing rapid oxide spallation, the benefits may diminish.
fields.uncertainty: The exact influence of micro-dimple geometry (size, depth, density) on the wear and deformation mechanisms is uncertain and requires optimization.

fields.hypothesis: Heat treatment that induces a gradient nanocrystalline subsurface in the FeNiCrCoCu coating will promote the development of a continuous, dense oxide (glaze) layer during high-temperature sliding, thereby improving wear resistance and accommodating plastic deformation.
fields.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating with a relatively homogeneous, coarse or moderately refined microstructure and non-uniform in situ oxide formation.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition high-temperature annealing treatment (e.g., a hold at an intermediate temperature below the melting point but high enough to drive partial recrystallization) to induce a depth-dependent refinement, forming a top nanocrystalline (NC) tribo-layer transitioning to an ultra-fine grained (UFG) region beneath.
fields.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (typically in the 600–800 °C regime) in ambient (or controlled oxidizing) atmosphere where tribo-oxidation can occur.
fields.structural_mediator: A gradient nanostructured (NC-to-UFG) subsurface that facilitates gradual stress relaxation and simultaneously promotes a continuous, dense oxide glaze layer.
fields.mechanism: The refined NC layer at the immediate surface enhances hardness and elevates the H/E and H3/E2 ratios, while the gradual grain size increase underneath minimizes sharp strain demarcations during sliding. In parallel, the enhanced grain boundary density accelerates tribo-oxidation kinetics to form a stable glaze layer that prevents direct adhesive contact. Together, these factors reduce abrasive damage and delamination under high-temperature wear.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the annealed coating should exhibit a markedly lower wear rate (by at least an order of magnitude similar to trends seen in nanohierarchical architectures) and reduced groove formation with fewer wear debris under high-temperature sliding conditions.
fields.baseline: The unannealed FeNiCrCoCu coating exhibiting less gradient structural evolution and a sporadic, discontinuous oxide layer.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in high-temperature regimes (≥600 °C) where oxidation kinetics are favorable, but may not be effective at significantly lower temperatures where oxide formation is minimal.
fields.uncertainty: Exact temperature and time parameters for optimal gradient formation in FeNiCrCoCu are uncertain, and the balance between softening and oxide layer stability must be tuned.

fields.hypothesis: Pre-sliding surface nano-texturing via controlled low-energy ion bombardment of the FeNiCrCoCu coating will create a nano-dimpled morphology that enhances tribo-oxidation uniformity and stress distribution under high-temperature sliding, thereby reducing wear and mitigating localized plastic deformation.
fields.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy thin coating with a smooth, as-deposited surface.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled low-energy ion bombardment treatment to the coated surface to generate a patterned nano-textured surface (e.g., an ordered array of nano-dimples) prior to service.
fields.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (600–800 °C) in an oxidizing or ambient atmosphere where tribo-oxidation is active during wear.
fields.structural_mediator: A pre-engineered nano-textured interface that enhances local stress redistribution and serves as a scaffold for more uniform and adherent glaze layer formation during sliding.
fields.mechanism: The nano-dimples act as controlled stress concentrators that can dissipate localized sliding stresses through more uniform dislocation motion and aid in the accelerated formation of a continuous oxide layer via tribo-oxidation. This adaptive surface morphology reduces the likelihood of abrupt plastic deformation, spalling, and debris generation, thus leading to improved wear resistance.
fields.predicted_outcome: In comparison with the untreated, smooth baseline coating, the nano-textured coating is anticipated to exhibit a lower friction coefficient, shallower wear tracks, and fewer signs of localized plastic instabilities during high-temperature sliding tests.
fields.baseline: A conventionally processed, smooth FeNiCrCoCu coating without any surface nano-texturing.

fields.structural_mediator: A uniformly pre-formed, adherent oxide scale that covers the coating surface.
fields.mechanism: By pre-forming a controlled oxide layer, the coating enters the sliding test with an already stable lubricating film. This continuous oxide film reduces metal-to-metal contact, limits adhesive wear, and minimizes the initiation of plastic deformation, analogous to how a continuous oxide layer on fine-grained HEAs assists in wear resistance [PMC9960858::web::016::3_4_worn_track_morphology_and_wear_mecha].
fields.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized coating is expected to show a lower friction coefficient and reduced specific wear rate during high-temperature sliding compared to a coating that relies on in-situ, uncontrolled oxidation.
fields.baseline: The typical FeNiCrCoCu coating without a pre-oxidation treatment, forming less uniform or discontinuous oxide layers during sliding.
fields.boundary: The improved performance is anticipated at temperatures and loads where oxidation plays a dominant role in wear; if the oxidation kinetics are too slow or the oxide film spalls off rapidly under sliding, the benefit might be reduced.
fields.uncertainty: The ideal parameters for the oxidation treatment (temperature, time, atmosphere) need to be optimized; the degree of improvement may vary and is somewhat uncertain without preliminary optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples on identical substrates: one set receiving the pre-oxidation treatment and one without the treatment. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding tests and assess friction behavior, oxide film integrity (with SEM/EDS), and wear rates.
measurements: Friction coefficient evolution
Specific wear rate via 3D surface profilometry
Surface oxide morphology and adhesion via SEM/EDS after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coating does not exhibit a continuous oxide film during sliding or if the friction and wear measurements are not statistically improved over the baseline coating, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

pool.label: C15
pool.builds_on: the understanding that processing-induced microstructural stresses and density can significantly affect wear behavior, extending traditional thermal spray coatings to cold spray methods.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces an alternative processing route (cold spraying) to impart beneficial residual stresses and microstructural features that have not been explored for the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy coating in the context of high-temperature sliding.

fields.hypothesis: Depositing the FeNiCrCoCu coating using cold spray instead of conventional thermal spraying will induce beneficial residual compressive stresses and a denser, less oxidized microstructure that governs improved wear resistance and reduced microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
fields.material_initial_state: A conventional thermally sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating that typically contains moderate porosity and in situ oxidation due to high-temperature particle melting.
fields.intervention: Switch the deposition method from thermal spraying to cold spraying, which operates at lower temperatures and imparts residual compressive stresses in the coating.
fields.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions where both plasma-induced oxidation and plastic deformation under mechanical load affect wear behavior.
fields.structural_mediator: A dense microstructure with elevated residual compressive stresses and lower pre-existing oxide content.
fields.mechanism: Cold spraying deposits the FeNiCrCoCu coating in a solid-state process, minimizing in-flight oxidation and maintaining low porosity. The rapid particle deformation upon impact creates residual compressive stresses that impede crack initiation and plastic flow during sliding, thereby reducing wear rates. This mechanism leverages the well-known benefits of compressive stresses in retarding fracture and plastic deformation [KG::wear_rate::c96d4a29fb].
fields.predicted_outcome: The cold-sprayed coating should exhibit a lower friction coefficient and reduced specific wear rate under high-temperature sliding compared to the conventional thermally sprayed counterpart.
fields.baseline: The standard thermally sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating deposited under high-temperature conditions.
fields.boundary: The advantages are expected to be most pronounced in sliding tests where thermal effects do not negate the residual stresses. However, at extremely high temperatures, residual stresses may relax, limiting the benefit.
fields.uncertainty: While compressive residual stresses and improved density are known to enhance wear performance, the magnitude of improvement in the specific FeNiCrCoCu system under high-temperature sliding is uncertain without direct comparative tests.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings: one deposited by conventional thermal spray and the other by cold spray. Subject both coatings to identical high-temperature sliding tests, then measure friction coefficients, wear rates, and evaluate residual stress and microstructural density using X-ray diffraction and microscopy.
measurements: Friction coefficient during sliding
Specific wear rate via 3D profilometry
Residual stress profiling (e.g., using XRD)
Microstructural examination (density, porosity) using SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cold-sprayed coating does not display residual compressive stresses, higher density, and statistically improved wear resistance relative to the thermally sprayed coating, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C2
top3.builds_on: the finding that nanohierarchical architectures with composition undulation promote adaptive friction interface protection by generating gradient structural layers and continuous glaze layers (PMC10241162).
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies controlled post-deposition heat treatment to the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy coating to explicitly induce depth-dependent grain refinement and facilitate optimized high-temperature oxide layer formation—an approach not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Heat treatment that induces a gradient nanocrystalline subsurface in the FeNiCrCoCu coating will promote the development of a continuous, dense oxide (glaze) layer during high-temperature sliding, thereby improving wear resistance and accommodating plastic deformation.
fields.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating with a relatively homogeneous, coarse or moderately refined microstructure and non-uniform in situ oxide formation.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition high-temperature annealing treatment (e.g., a hold at an intermediate temperature below the melting point but high enough to drive partial recrystallization) to induce a depth-dependent refinement, forming a top nanocrystalline (NC) tribo-layer transitioning to an ultra-fine grained (UFG) region beneath.
fields.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (typically in the 600–800 °C regime) in ambient (or controlled oxidizing) atmosphere where tribo-oxidation can occur.
fields.structural_mediator: A gradient nanostructured (NC-to-UFG) subsurface that facilitates gradual stress relaxation and simultaneously promotes a continuous, dense oxide glaze layer.
fields.mechanism: The refined NC layer at the immediate surface enhances hardness and elevates the H/E and H3/E2 ratios, while the gradual grain size increase underneath minimizes sharp strain demarcations during sliding. In parallel, the enhanced grain boundary density accelerates tribo-oxidation kinetics to form a stable glaze layer that prevents direct adhesive contact. Together, these factors reduce abrasive damage and delamination under high-temperature wear.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the annealed coating should exhibit a markedly lower wear rate (by at least an order of magnitude similar to trends seen in nanohierarchical architectures) and reduced groove formation with fewer wear debris under high-temperature sliding conditions.
fields.baseline: The unannealed FeNiCrCoCu coating exhibiting less gradient structural evolution and a sporadic, discontinuous oxide layer.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in high-temperature regimes (≥600 °C) where oxidation kinetics are favorable, but may not be effective at significantly lower temperatures where oxide formation is minimal.
fields.uncertainty: Exact temperature and time parameters for optimal gradient formation in FeNiCrCoCu are uncertain, and the balance between softening and oxide layer stability must be tuned.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical substrates: one set receives the controlled post-deposition annealing to develop a gradient nanostructure and the other remains as-deposited. Subject both to identical high-temperature (600–800 °C) sliding wear tests in the same oxidizing environment.
measurements: Wear rate (mm3/Nm) via profilometry
Coefficient of friction (COF)
Cross-sectional microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to verify gradient structure and glaze layer continuity
Nanoindentation to measure local H and E values
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and improved stress accommodation (as indicated by more uniform H/E profiles and thicker, continuous glaze layers) compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C13
top3.builds_on: the observation that fine-grained HEAs have superior wear resistance due to high surface strength [PMC9960858::web::017::3_4_worn_track_morphology_and_wear_mecha]
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces grain boundary stabilization via Y addition to ensure the fine-grained structure is thermally stable during operation—a step beyond simply refining the microstructure.

fields.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (~0.5–1 at.%) of a grain boundary stabilizer such as yttrium (Y) to the FeNiCrCoCu feedstock will inhibit grain coarsening during high-temperature operation and thereby retain a fine, thermally stable microstructure that improves wear resistance and minimizes localized deformation during sliding.
fields.material_initial_state: A thermally sprayed FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with a baseline grain structure that is initially refined but prone to coarsening at high temperatures.
fields.intervention: Introduce ~0.5–1 at.% yttrium in the feedstock prior to spraying.
fields.conditions: High-temperature sliding in an oxidizing atmosphere where frictional heating could otherwise lead to grain coarsening and softening.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure with yttrium segregated at grain boundaries that pin the boundaries against thermal coarsening.
fields.mechanism: The yttrium is expected to segregate to the grain boundaries during deposition and subsequent service. Its presence will provide a pinning force that retards grain-boundary migration and coarsening when the coating is exposed to high-temperature sliding. This retention of fine grains maintains high hardness and better resistance to dislocation motion, similar to the observed benefits in fine-grained HEAs [PMC9960858::web::009::3_1_microstructure_characterization_of_c].
fields.predicted_outcome: The Y-doped coating should exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced specific wear rates (i.e. improved wear resistance) under high-temperature sliding compared to the baseline coating that lacks such stabilization.
fields.baseline: The standard thermally sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating without any grain boundary stabilizers.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected in high-temperature regimes where thermally activated grain growth is significant; if the operating temperature is too low, the impact of Y addition may be negligible.
fields.uncertainty: While the principles of grain boundary pinning are well-established, the exact quantitative improvement in wear performance is uncertain and will depend on the Y distribution and concentration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings: one using standard feedstock and one doped with ~0.5–1 at.% Y. Subject both coatings to high-temperature sliding tests under identical conditions, then analyze grain size evolution (using SEM/EBSD), friction coefficient histories, and wear rates.
measurements: Grain size distribution before and after sliding
Evolution of friction coefficient during sliding
Specific wear rate via profilometry and microstructural examination of wear tracks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped coating shows no statistically significant retention of fine grains or does not exhibit a reduced friction coefficient and specific wear rate compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C10
top3.builds_on: The observation in the AlCrFeNiV study that oxide formation—although occurring as a wear byproduct—can affect wear mechanisms, combined with established principles of oxide dispersion strengthening from materials science literature.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis intentionally integrates controlled oxygen doping during the deposition of FeNiCrCoCu to create a beneficial oxide dispersion in-situ, a novel approach that differentiates it from both traditional precipitation hardening and from the dual-phase strategies considered in the AlCrFeNiV work.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled, low level of oxygen during the deposition of the FeNiCrCoCu coating will promote the in-situ formation of finely dispersed oxide nanoparticles (such as Cr-based oxides) within the metallic matrix. These nano-oxides will act as stable dispersion-strengthening phases that hinder dislocation motion and arrest microcrack propagation during high-temperature sliding, thereby governing improved wear resistance and mitigating microscopic deformation.
fields.material_initial_state: A conventional, oxygen-free, equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with a uniform metallic microstructure.
fields.intervention: Adjust the deposition atmosphere to incorporate a controlled trace oxygen partial pressure (at a level low enough to prevent bulk oxidation) during coating formation, so that a small volume fraction of oxide nanoparticles is formed uniformly within the matrix.
fields.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests in an environment where frictional heating and oxidation are active (e.g., temperatures in the range of 500–700 °C), thereby testing the stability and mechanical contribution of the oxide dispersion.
fields.structural_mediator: A dispersion of nanoscale oxide particles, likely Cr-oxides, uniformly embedded within the metallic FeNiCrCoCu matrix. These particles are expected to pin dislocations and impede the coalescence of microcracks.
fields.mechanism: The controlled oxygen leads to a limited in-situ oxidation reaction during deposition, yielding finely dispersed oxide nanoparticles. These nanoparticles act as obstacles to dislocation movement (dispersion strengthening) and serve to blunt or arrest crack tips during mechanical sliding, thus reducing wear and microscopic deformation. This mechanism leverages the observation (in the AlCrFeNiV study) that oxide formation occurs during wear but proactively integrates beneficial oxide phases into the untested high-temperature regime.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline oxygen-free coating, the oxygen-doped coating should exhibit a lower wear rate and a reduction in microcrack density or surface delamination when subjected to high-temperature sliding tests. The benefit is anticipated to be significant if the oxide particle size and distribution remain within an optimal nanoscale range.
fields.baseline: An as-deposited, oxygen-free FeNiCrCoCu coating fabricated under inert atmosphere conditions.
fields.boundary: The positive effect is contingent upon maintaining oxygen levels within a narrow range. Excess oxygen may lead to deleterious bulk oxidation or formation of brittle phases, while too little oxygen may fail to produce an adequate dispersion of oxide nanoparticles.
fields.uncertainty: While oxide dispersion strengthening is a well-known mechanism, the precise nature (composition, size, volume fraction) of the in-situ formed oxides in the FeNiCrCoCu system and their quantitative effect on wear resistance under high-temperature sliding remain to be carefully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of coatings: one deposited under a controlled low-oxygen atmosphere to promote oxide nanoparticle formation, and a control group deposited under strictly inert conditions. Characterize both groups via TEM/EDS to evaluate the presence, size, and distribution of oxide particles, then perform high-temperature sliding wear tests to compare wear rates and microscopic deformation features.
measurements: TEM/EDS for nanoparticle characterization
XRD for phase identification
Wear rate and friction coefficient measurements during sliding tests
Surface microscopy (SEM) of post-wear features to assess crack density and delamination
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped coatings do not exhibit a distinct, beneficial dispersion of oxide nanoparticles, or if their wear performance and microscopic deformation characteristics are not significantly improved relative to the oxygen-free baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
